Agent Attention — One Model, One Place

Analysis·budding·implemented·JUL 21, 2026

When an agent finishes or asks a question, kolu plays a sound, shows a popup, badges the app icon, and marks the dock and host tab. This note picks one word for it — attention — writes down the rules, and records that they now live in one place, plus the follow-ups the review left open.

Contents

  • The rules — one set, every host
  • One word: attention
  • How it’s built
  • Effective finish — agent state fused with terminal quiet
  • Follow-ups

When an agent finishes a turn, or stops to ask you a question, kolu reacts: a sound, an OS popup, an app-icon badge, a host-tab mark, a dock dot. That is all one thing — getting your attention — and it now lives in one model, in one place.

The rules — one set, every host

One set of rules, identical on every host. The only thing “which host you’re looking at” changes is whether a terminal counts as already seen.

Agent state Sound + popup (once) On-screen marks Goes away when
Asking you (waiting for input) if not already seen loud amber host-tab count + dock pip you answer
Just finished (no input needed, PTY gone quiet) if not already seen quiet dim-amber host-tab dot + dock unread you look at it
Working / idle — (optional “live” ring) —

The two host-tab marks speak one amber “needs you” language in two tiers: the full-amber count for asking (blocking, actionable) and a dim-amber dot for an unseen finish (a lesser nudge) — never a separate grey vocabulary.The dot reads the cross-host unseen-finished mark useAttention publishes, not the raw finishedIds — a finished agent idles in waiting ~forever, so “has any finished agent” would light every host permanently. The unseen rule is the pure, unit-tested nextUnseenFinished. “Which host” enters in exactly one place — seen: a terminal you’re staring at is seen; one on a background host isn’t. Everything else is host-agnostic.

One word: attention

The code used to call this three things — alerts, attention, notifications. Now it’s one word, attention: the system that decides when a terminal needs you and how to show it. Notification is kept for one thing only — the OS/browser popup (the platform’s own Notification API), a channel attention uses, not the concept.

How it’s built

One useAttention module owns the rules. Underneath it: a pure attentionTransitions decides “needs you now” vs “just finished” (unit-tested, off the wire); delivery — the sound and OS popup — rides the existing attentionNotify seam packages/client/src/attentionNotify.ts; and agent-state → class stays in the shared agentProjection fold packages/terminal-vocab/src/agentProjection.ts. Every host reads its own urgency cell (now carrying finishedIds too), so a background host’s finished agent pings and shows a quiet mark exactly like the active host’s — the behavior that used to be missing.

Before, the rules were split across three modules by whether you were looking at the host — useTerminalAlerts (active host), useHostAttention (the others), and an active-only “seen” ledger — so the same agent behaved differently depending on focus. Those are gone. Shipped in #1931; the activityAlerts setting was renamed attentionAlerts (with a migration).

Effective finish — agent state fused with terminal quiet

An agent like Claude Code can mark its turn finished while background sub-agents keep working, so a raw waiting is a premature “finished” — the transcript says done, but the terminal is still moving bytes. The fix: a waiting terminal is only an effective finish once its PTY has gone quiet for a debounce window (~5s). The gate byte-taps only the waiting terminals — a small, bounded set — debounces each on the same tracker the live-dot uses packages/padi/src/terminalActivityTracker.ts, and feeds the settled set into the urgency fold, which admits a waiting terminal to finishedIds only when settled. packages/padi/src/urgency.ts

Three decisions make it correct. It lives in padi, not the client live-dot useTerminalActivity (which only sees attached tiles) — padi sees every terminal’s bytes, active or background, so the whole cross-host model rides it. packages/padi/src/finishGate.ts It’s default-excluded — a terminal that just flipped to waiting isn’t yet settled, so a late observation only delays a finish (the lesser, non-blocking nudge), it can never fire one early. And it gates finished only: the ASKING path (awaiting_user) is blocking and actionable, so it fires at once, never debounced. Because “output stopped” is a non-event on the wire, the gate carries its own debounce timer and pushes the quiet-crossing edge into the reactor graph so urgency re-folds. It’s a heuristic tuned by the quiet window: a chatty background agent is caught, and an agent whose TUI redraws at rest (a spinner emitting real bytes) would defer a real finish. Shipped in #1938.

Follow-ups

What the review gauntlet surfaced but the first cut left out. Items marked user-facing change what you see or hear; the rest are internal quality or CI infra.

Correctness

  • Split-aware “seen”. (user-facing) The seen check compares the active tile id, so a finished pane you can plainly see inside a split can still chime. The right test is “a visible pane of the active tile,” not tile-or-focus alone. packages/client/src/attention/useAttention.ts
  • Test the real path. e2e drives a simulate hook that bypasses the detect→fire engine — the exact gap that let a reconcile-mutation bug ship. The engine has unit tests now; an e2e over the real agent-state → deliver path would close the class.

Robustness

  • Route notification-popup clicks through the deep-link resolver. (user-facing) Clicking the OS/PWA notification popup — the banner the service worker shows when an agent needs you and you’re not looking (it can arrive with kolu backgrounded or closed) — today calls a raw tile activation. Routing it through the same resolver #/t/… deep links use would land the right split, survive a cold boot (the app was closed when the popup arrived), and report a terminal that’s since gone. packages/client/src/attention/useAttention.ts
  • Carry membership in the urgency cell. (user-facing, only if it bites) A terminal first seen already-finished (a wake, another tab) can’t be told from a real finish, because working terminals are invisible to the cell.

Structure

  • Fold the app-badge painter’s ordering/dedup/retry into @kolu/surface-app’s setAttention seam and route through it, dropping the app-local copy.
  • Export surface-map’s WatchedValue liveness so useAttention stops duplicating it.
  • Move the e2e-only AttentionDeps fields off the production seam.
  • Model the finish gate’s per-terminal lifecycle as a type, not six sets. The gate tracks each terminal across six parallel keyed collections — tracked, taps, tapGen, attached, settled, awaitingRearm packages/padi/src/finishGate.ts — whose invariants (settled ⟹ attached; settled ∧ awaitingRearm never co-hold) are enforced by call-order discipline, documented in prose. A single Map<TerminalId, TapState> with a discriminated TapState would make the illegal combinations unspellable at the type level. Deferred, not done: the state is a genuine product (attachment × episode × quiet) plus per-tap metadata (tapGen, the disposer) that coexists with every arm, so it isn’t a clean single discriminant — and the current form is quiet-window-timing sensitive, thoroughly unit-tested (incl. the F1/F3/F5 edges), and freshly hardened through the review, so the rewrite is a follow-up to weigh carefully rather than churn to force now.

CI hygiene — the recurring darwin flake

The darwin code-tab fs-watch scenarios flake because odu leaks temp checkouts and orphaned e2e processes on the macOS CI boxes, and the leaks peg fseventsd. A post-run temp-dir + orphaned-process reap (plus hardening the file-watch waitFors — a retry doesn’t touch the wedged fseventsd layer) would stop it recurring every darwin run. Not attention code, but it’s what turns a green PR red.
